newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's budget envisions surplus in 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's budget envisions surplus in 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton will propose government spending of $1.69 trillion for fiscal 1998, aiming to gradually eliminate the deficit and arrive at a $17 billion surplus in 2002, according to a summary of the budget obtained by reporters on Wednesday.

The full budget will be made public by the White House on Thursday morning. The summary document showed the deficit in the current 1997 fiscal year will be $125.6 billion, up from the $107.3 billion deficit posted last year. The deficit is expected to start falling in 1998 and reach a surplus in 2002. The government is expected to spend $1.63 trillion in the current fiscal year.

While government spending will continue to rise to the year 20002, the White House projects revenues will increase as well -- from $1.57 trillion expected in fiscal 1998 to $1.90 trillion in fiscal 2002. The government is expected to receive $1.51 trillion in the current 1997 fiscal year.

Clinton will propose a five year tax cut worth $98.4 billion in tax cuts to be offset by closing tax loopholes worth $34.3 billion over the same 1998-2002 period. His budget also expects $36.1 billion will be raised from the auction of broadcasting rights and expects to raise $41.7 billion from other sources such as renewed excise taxes and other user fees.

As expected, his budget will seek to cut $100 billion over five years from Medicare, the health insurance program for the elderly, and forecasts a slight $9.3 billion cut in the Medicaid health program for the poor over the same period.

Clinton's budget forecasts the economy on a steady growth path of 2.0 percent for 1997 and 1998, with a projection it would strenghten to 2.3 percent from 1999 through 2002. Unemployment was expected to reach 5.3 percent in 1997 and then was seem rising to 5.5 percent in 1998. Inflation was forecast at 2.6 percent this year and to rise to 2.7 percent in 1998.
